title: Draft: feat(minder): report policy matches as AI audit events
description:
## Description

This MR reports each GitLab policy match that the Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook makes to GitLab as an AI audit event, so that audit mode policies work and local enforcement shows in the audit trail. It is the first MR for https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/634683 and is stacked on https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli/-/merge_requests/4467. GitLab stores the events once https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/272022 is merged. Until then GitLab drops the unknown event type without an error, so sending early is safe.

After the hook prints its decision, it records every policy that matched the tool call, including policies in audit mode that print nothing. The records go to a spool file per session in the glab configuration directory, under `gaig/policy-decisions`. The folder is readable only by the user. The hook makes no network call, writes once per tool call, and stops writing when a session's spool reaches 1 MiB. If recording fails, the hook still prints the same decision and exits 0. A record cut off by a full disk or a killed hook does not damage the next one.

`glab minder audit sync` uploads the records as `ai_tool_call_policy_matched` events whenever it syncs a Claude Code session, from the Stop hook and from the periodic sync. Decision uploads are independent of transcript uploads. The sync first posts the transcript events and saves its place in the transcript, and only then posts the decisions in their own requests. A decision that GitLab refuses therefore never stops or repeats the transcript upload, and a failed decision upload is reported as a warning without failing the sync. If GitLab refuses an event for good, with a 4xx answer other than a rate limit, a timeout, or a refused token, glab posts the rest of the request again without it, so only that event is dropped and the other decisions are posted. When GitLab also refuses the first and last event of a request on their own, glab drops the whole request, and one sync makes at most 20 extra requests to find refused events, so a GitLab that refuses every request cannot cost a request per event. After a failure that can pass, such as a network error, a server error, a rate limit, or a refused token, glab keeps all of the session's decisions and the next sync posts them again. When the periodic sync is installed, the session is not marked as completed until its decisions are posted, so that the periodic sync, which skips completed sessions, still uploads them. Without it, the hook completes the session anyway and the kept decisions are deleted with the session's local state. Decisions older than the 89 days GitLab accepts are dropped, so a session completes even if they never post. Each event has a stable ID, so an event sent twice is stored once.

The sync renames the spool aside before reading it, so the hook never waits for the sync and matches recorded during an upload are kept for the next one. This also holds when the Stop hook and the periodic sync run at the same time. A session with new matches syncs even when its transcript has nothing new. The spool is deleted together with the rest of the session's local state, and spools of sessions that no hook recorded are deleted after 30 days.

Redaction: the hook records the Bash command or the file path as the agent sent it. It keeps the first 32 KB, replaces common secrets with glab's redaction markers, and then cuts the result to 1 KB. Secrets are replaced before the 1 KB cut, so a secret cut in half cannot leak its first part. MCP tool input is never recorded, only the server and tool names. The command or path is still sent in full, up to 8 KB, with the tool call's own audit event. The copy in this event is only there so the policy match can be read on its own.

The event details have these keys: `policy_id`, `policy_version`, `policy_name`, `policy_mode`, `policy_action`, `policy_decision`, `rule_index`, `tool_name`, `tool_call_id`, `target`, `file_operation`, `mcp_server`, `mcp_tool`, `input`, `input_truncated`, and `agent_name`. Keys without a value are left out.

## How has this been tested?

Unit tests cover the hook writing one record per match, audit mode matches, writing nothing when no policy matches, the size cap, redaction and the 1 KB cut for long and very long commands, stable event IDs, and the hook printing the same decision when it cannot record. Spool tests cover claims, releases, failed uploads, unreadable and cut off lines, a full spool that a sync claims, and matches recorded while one or two syncs run. Sync tests run against a fake GitLab and check the event names, details and IDs, removal after success, that only the decision GitLab refuses for good is dropped while the other decisions and the transcript still upload, that decisions are kept after server errors, rate limits and refused tokens, that a session is completed only once its kept decisions are posted, or right away when no periodic sync would complete it, that a GitLab refusing every request costs a bounded number of requests, that decisions posted again after a failure are not counted twice, a match recorded during the upload, uploads without new transcript entries, the age limit, and the removal of spools of forgotten sessions. I ran the govern tests with shuffling and with the race detector, golangci-lint, and go vet for Windows. A new benchmark shows no change for calls without a match and about 0.1 ms more for calls with one.
